ov: A play set over Christmas and New Year 1967–68 that follows three families as they leave home for holidays and find themselves face to face with grief, class, death and hope. Shakespeare’s A Midsummer Night’s Dream opens the play and King Lear closes it, and the theatre itself becomes a way of healing. In the Common Module it shows how people cope with loss, why strength is more than stoicism, and how vulnerability can bring people together.
rub: Language, forms and features: dramatic structure, dialogue, stage directions, metatheatre, symbol (storm, shells, sea) and the Shakespearean frame.
Emotional and lived experience: grief, illness, class and family conflict.
Agency and conformity: characters rehearse social roles (the headmaster, the controlling mother) before dropping them.
sum: At a school performance of A Midsummer Night’s Dream, the headmaster Roy and the teacher Miss Latrobe prepare for the holidays. Tom, who played Puck, is a gentle boy whose parents Vic and Harry are taking him on a last family holiday; Meg, Tom’s schoolmate, goes camping with her controlling mother Gwen and her father Jim; and Roy and his grieving wife Coral, who lost a son in the war, fly to a luxury hotel on the Gold Coast. Roy insists on stoicism, Gwen on control, and each family’s holiday exposes the cracks. A storm shakes them all. Coral crosses into the dark and meets a young man, Rick; Gwen and Jim’s van is wrecked; Meg guides them to a beach where the families meet; and Tom and Coral stage a mermaid story that expresses grief. At the end Gwen and Jim embrace, Roy accepts Coral’s grief, and Miss Latrobe begins reading King Lear with her students under the trees.
acts: The school play ends and the teachers and parents part for the holidays. We meet Tom, Meg and their families, and see how class and expectation separate them. Roy and Coral are bound for the Gold Coast.
The families prepare to leave. Gwen, Jim and Meg argue over their Christmas rituals; Tom and his mother Vic talk quietly the night before they go away.
At the Gold Coast hotel Coral breaks down and meets Rick in the dark, while Roy tells her to carry on. At the camping ground Meg confronts Gwen. The fairies stage a storm that empties the stage.

After the storm the families regroup. Gwen and Jim’s van and boat are wrecked, and Meg guides them to a beach where Tom’s family is staying. Tom and Coral perform a mermaid story at the campers’ night, and the families watch a bonfire.
Gwen and Jim reconcile with the gift of slippers; Coral gives Roy a handful of shells. In the schoolyard Miss Latrobe’s class begins to read King Lear.
ch: Tom
Schoolboy who played Puck
Witty, observant and sensitive. His mother’s lines show that this is a last holiday. His humour is courage.
Better I am unhappy for all eternity than she suffer another moment.
Meg
Gwen and Jim’s daughter
Observant and unafraid to challenge her mother. She connects with Tom and guides her family to the beach.
There’s always something we do wrong that takes you weeks to forgive.
Gwen
Meg’s mother
Controlling and anxious about appearances; her bitterness hides loneliness. She softens by the end.
Christmas is only for the young ones, anyway.
Jim
Gwen’s husband
Mild and patient, he keeps the peace and communicates through small gestures (the slippers).
It’s only old presents. Slippers and your new bread knife.
Roy
Headmaster; Coral’s husband
Public face of authority and stoicism. He tries to master his grief with practicality.
That’s what history is, people picking themselves up, pulling themselves together and going on.
Coral
Roy’s wife; grieving mother
Haunted by her son’s death in war. She seeks connection, even in strangers.
You’re still alive. You’re still alive and talking and laughing.
Vic
Tom’s mother
Warm, protective and quietly strained. She guides Tom to “pretend” for his father’s sake.
You can act, we all know that now.
Harry
Tom’s father
A traditional father whom his family tries to shield from sadness.
(Vic) Your father will enjoy this trip.
Miss Latrobe
Teacher
A figure of Shakespeare and teaching, whose idealism frames the play’s start and end.
it is the struggle between man and nature, as well as between man and man, and between man and himself
Rick
Young man Coral meets
Confused and unsettled, he sees his life as meaningless.
Everything I do is wrong. But I can’t help myself.
cx: Michael Gow is an Australian playwright and director, born in 1955. Away draws on his love of theatre and on his sense of the impact of illness, grief and war on ordinary families. Check your class notes for details of the play’s first productions.

The play uses Shakespeare’s A Midsummer Night’s Dream and King Lear as a frame, suggesting that theatre can heal. Australian summer holiday rituals (caravan parks, a hotel on the Gold Coast, Christmas presents) reveal class differences. The fairies and the storm borrow from Shakespeare’s world of magic and tempest.

The play takes place in the summer of 1967–68, in the middle of Australia’s involvement in the Vietnam War. Conscription (national service) sent young men to fight, which is why Coral and Roy have lost a son “in war”. The disappearance of Prime Minister Harold Holt in December 1967 deepened a sense of national uncertainty.

Class divides (the luxury hotel versus the camping ground), expectations of stoic masculinity (Roy) and rigid femininity (Gwen), the pressure to keep up appearances, and the stigma of illness and grief.
im: The storm: the fairies “stage a spectacular storm”, a magic and symbolic tempest that clears the stage and breaks the families’ defences.
The sea, the beach and the bonfire: the setting where the families meet; the bonfire that Vic compares to the coming of the Armada becomes a communal ritual.
The shells and the hat: Coral lifts a handful of shells from her hat and Roy buries his face in them, a silent gesture of acceptance.
The mermaid story: Tom’s tale, with Coral as a mermaid, turns grief into theatre and love into sacrifice.
th: Grief must be felt, not suppressed. Coral’s breakdown and Roy’s eventual acceptance show healing as shared.

Holiday choices reveal social positions, and the families learn they share the same fears.
Gifts, rituals and silences show how families hide and reveal love.
Common Module: paradoxes of motivation and behaviour.

A.i: In Michael Gow’s Away, audiences are offered the opportunity to examine assumptions about human strength and vulnerability by watching families who equate strength with stoicism and control gradually discover that healing begins in exposure. Set against the Vietnam War era of 1967 and framed by Shakespeare’s A Midsummer Night’s Dream and King Lear, the play uses dramatic irony, stage image and metatheatre to suggest that vulnerability, expressed and shared, is the truest form of strength.
b: Gow first exposes the assumption that strength means stoicism. When Coral breaks down in grief for her son killed in war, Roy lectures her: “That’s what history is, people picking themselves up, pulling themselves together and going on. We can’t stop.” The list of verbs and the authoritative tone present resilience as denial, and his confidence is shaken when Coral’s “[a great cry]”, “You sent him away!”, shatters politeness. Gow’s stage directions bring raw emotion into the open, positioning the audience to see that Roy’s strength is a fragile performance.

He then shows how vulnerability can be disguised as control. Gwen’s bitter “Christmas is only for the young ones, anyway” conceals loneliness behind sarcasm, while Meg’s accusation, “There’s always something we do wrong that takes you weeks to forgive”, exposes the family’s habit of silence and resentment. Gwen’s need to control is a defence against fear, and the playwright’s dialogue reveals how rigid roles prevent intimacy. The play challenges the assumption that those who dominate are strong.

Finally, Gow suggests that strength is found in shared theatre and selfless love. Tom’s mermaid tale, “Better I am unhappy for all eternity than she suffer another moment”, turns sacrifice into story, and Vic’s remark, “You can act, we all know that now”, shows performance as a way of coping. In the final moments, Coral gives Roy a handful of shells and he “buries his face in the shells”, a silent gesture of acceptance. Jim’s gift of slippers to Gwen likewise replaces words with care. Strength emerges through gestures of tenderness.
A.c: Ultimately, Gow challenges audiences to reconsider what it means to be strong. By ending with Miss Latrobe’s class reading King Lear, a play about a man who learns humility through suffering, Away suggests that facing grief, illness and each other is the real courage.
A.n: What to notice: the thesis names the assumption (strength as stoicism) and the dramatic techniques; each paragraph pairs a character’s speech with a stage direction or technique; the dramatic form is analysed, not only the dialogue; the conclusion links to the play’s Shakespearean frame.

B.i: In Away, Michael Gow shows that strength and vulnerability are connected. The play follows three families on holiday who must deal with grief and conflict.
b: Roy tries to be strong when Coral is grieving. He says, “That’s what history is, people picking themselves up, pulling themselves together and going on.” This shows he thinks strength is about not showing emotion. But Coral shouts, “You sent him away!”, which shows she is hurting.

Gwen is also trying to be strong. She says, “Christmas is only for the young ones, anyway.” This shows that she is lonely. Meg tells her, “There’s always something we do wrong that takes you weeks to forgive”, which shows that Gwen is hard to live with.
At the end, Coral gives Roy shells and he buries his face in them. This shows they are closer. Gwen and Jim also hug, which shows they have changed.
B.c: In conclusion, Gow shows that strength and vulnerability go together. The characters become stronger when they show their feelings.
B.n: What to notice: relevant evidence and a clear argument, but there is little attention to dramatic technique (stage directions, symbol, metatheatre), and explanations are general (“this shows…”).

models.C: In Away, Roy says that people have to keep going but Coral is sad. This shows that she is vulnerable. The playwright uses dialogue to show this.
models.D: Away is about families on holiday. They have problems. At the end they are happy.

A.i: Through the particular lives of Coral, Tom and Gwen, Michael Gow’s Away enriches our understanding of the endurance of the human spirit as a shared, performed and healing act. Written for the stage, the play uses Shakespearean allusion, symbol and ritual to show that people endure not through isolation but through story, play and gesture, inviting audiences to see theatre itself as a form of survival.
b: Coral’s life shows that endurance begins in facing grief. When she says to Rick, “You’re still alive. You’re still alive and talking and laughing”, the repetition shows how her loss colours every encounter. Her “[a great cry]”, “You sent him away!”, breaks Roy’s stoicism and exposes the cost of silence. By representing a grieving mother, Gow enriches our understanding of endurance as the courage to feel.

Tom’s life reveals endurance as creativity. His mother’s plea, “You can act, we all know that now”, turns performance into a way of bearing the unbearable, and the mermaid tale, “Better I am unhappy for all eternity than she suffer another moment”, makes sacrifice a story that others can share. Tom’s humour and play do not deny his situation; they transform it. The metatheatre of a play within a play shows the spirit enduring through imagination.

Gwen’s life shows that endurance includes change. Her bitter “Christmas is only for the young ones, anyway” gives way, at the close, to an embrace with Jim, who replaces speech with the gift of slippers. The bonfire that Vic likens to the coming of the Armada gathers the families as a community, and the closing reading of King Lear suggests a cycle: suffering will be faced again, but with shared language. Gow’s staging of reconciliation reveals that the spirit endures by remaining open to others.
A.c: Gow’s representation of these particular lives therefore deepens our understanding of the endurance of the human spirit. By turning grief into story and family into community, Away suggests that people survive by being seen and held, not by standing alone.
A.n: What to notice: “endurance” is defined (shared, performed, healing), each paragraph centres one particular life, and dramatic form (stage directions, metatheatre, symbol) is analysed alongside dialogue.

B.i: In Away, Michael Gow shows the endurance of the human spirit through the lives of Coral, Tom and Gwen. They all face hardship but find ways to keep going.
b: Coral is grieving her son. She says to Rick, “You’re still alive. You’re still alive and talking and laughing.” This shows she misses her son. She also shouts, “You sent him away!”, which shows she is hurting but is brave enough to say it.

Tom is ill but he keeps acting and joking. His mother says, “You can act, we all know that now.” His mermaid story, “Better I am unhappy for all eternity than she suffer another moment”, shows that he is caring.
Gwen changes at the end. She hugs Jim after he gives her slippers. This shows that she has become more open. Everyone meets at the beach, which shows that the families are connected.
B.c: In conclusion, Gow shows endurance through the characters who keep going and learn to show love.
B.n: What to notice: relevant evidence but mostly retelling. There is little discussion of form or technique (stage directions, metatheatre), and “enriches our understanding” is not addressed.

fc: A Midsummer Night’s Dream opens it and King Lear closes it.
Theatre that draws attention to itself as theatre. In Away: the school play, Tom’s mermaid tale and Miss Latrobe’s reading of King Lear.
Acceptance of grief: Coral gives Roy a handful and he buries his face in them.
What was happening in Australia in 1967–68?
The Vietnam War and conscription, which is why Coral and Roy have lost a son “in war”.
